passed.title: diff(null_behavior="drop") shortens the column and breaks with_columns
passed.trap: By default `Expr.diff` keeps the input length and puts `null` in the first `n` rows, like pandas. With `null_behavior="drop"` those rows are removed, so the result has `n` fewer rows. That shorter expression cannot be added next to the original columns with `DataFrame.with_columns`, which raises an error. Keep the default `"ignore"` when adding a column. Use `"drop"` only in a `DataFrame.select` where every output has the same shortened length.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [20, 10, 30, 25, 35]})

try:
    df.with_columns(d=pl.col("x").diff(null_behavior="drop"))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

# Right: keep the length (first row is null) when adding a column
print(df.with_columns(d=pl.col("x").diff()))

# "drop" is fine when the output stands alone
print(df.select(pl.col("x").diff(null_behavior="drop")))

passed.title: bitwise_and/or/xor are aggregations, not element-wise operators
passed.trap: `Expr.bitwise_and`, `Expr.bitwise_or` and `Expr.bitwise_xor` take no argument. Each one reduces a whole column (or each group) to a single value. Code like `pl.col("a").bitwise_and(pl.col("b"))` fails. Using it as a row-wise combine of two columns is wrong. For element-wise bit operations between two integer columns, use `Expr.and_`, `Expr.or_` and `Expr.xor`, or the operators `&`, `|` and `^`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [12, 10], "b": [10, 6]})

try:
    df.select(pl.col("a").bitwise_and(pl.col("b")))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

# bitwise_and reduces the column to ONE value: 12 & 10 = 8
print(df.select(pl.col("a").bitwise_and()))

# Element-wise: row by row a & b -> [8, 2]
print(df.select(pl.col("a").and_(pl.col("b")).alias("elementwise")))

passed.title: Out-of-domain trig results are NaN/inf, not null
passed.trap: The inverse trig functions always return Float64 and never raise for bad inputs. `Expr.arctanh` of 1.0 gives `inf`, and `Expr.arccos` of 2.0 gives NaN. Polars treats NaN as a float value, not as missing, so `Expr.is_null` and `Expr.fill_null` will not catch these results. Detect them with `Expr.is_nan` or `Expr.is_finite`. Convert them with `Expr.fill_nan(None)` if you want them to behave as nulls.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [0.5, 2.0, 1.0]})
res = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("a").arccos().alias("acos"),
    pl.col("a").arctanh().alias("atanh"),
)
print(res)
print(res.select(
    pl.col("acos").is_null().alias("acos_is_null"),
    pl.col("acos").is_nan().alias("acos_is_nan"),
    pl.col("atanh").is_finite().alias("atanh_finite"),
))
# Turn NaN into a real null so null handling applies
print(res.select(pl.col("acos").fill_nan(None).is_null()))

passed.title: cum_sum leaves null rows null and widens small ints to Int64
passed.trap: `Expr.cum_sum` and the other cumulative functions skip nulls, but the output is still `null` at those positions. It does not carry the running total forward, as a SQL running SUM would. If every row needs the total so far, chain `.fill_null(strategy="forward")`. `Expr.cum_sum` and `Expr.cum_prod` also cast Int8, UInt8, Int16 and UInt16 input to Int64. The output schema therefore differs from the input schema.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"v": [None, 10, None, 8]}, schema={"v": pl.Int8})
out = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("v").cum_sum().alias("cs"),
    pl.col("v").cum_sum().fill_null(strategy="forward").alias("cs_filled"),
)
print(out)
print(out.schema)
